tldr: By reformulating dynamic center of mass (capture point) relative to the support foot, unmeasurable base linear velocity cancels out, yielding an observable policy (DDC) that enables stable humanoid single-leg balance and zero-shot deployment to a real Unitree G1 without distillation.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed method. A single unified policy is trained via asymmetric FastSAC using support-foot-relative Dynamic-CoM observations and human postural control-inspired rewards, evaluated on a simulator-agnostic benchmark, and deployed directly to a real Unitree G1 without distillation.
overview:
In recent years, reinforcement learning policies for humanoid robots have mastered agile whole-body behaviors like dancing and backflips. Surprisingly, however, they fail completely at a basic requirement: staying balanced while standing still on one leg. When tested across 90 single-leg poses on our benchmark, eight released state-of-the-art general foundation policies held a clean single-leg stance on exactly zero motions (0/90). Most robots avoided falling only by hurriedly putting their lifted foot back down or hopping on their stance foot to recover from imbalance rather than preventing it.

Why is single-leg balance so difficult? Mechanically, preventing a fall requires controlling not just the center of mass (CoM) position, but also its extrapolated velocity—the capture point (xCoM). However, computing the capture point requires the absolute base linear velocity, which no on-board sensor (encoders or IMU) measures directly. Prior work has therefore confined this dynamic balance signal to privileged critics or teacher models, feeding the real-world actor only static CoM positions or relying on distillation.

This work breaks through the deployability barrier with an elegant change of reference frame. By expressing the relationship between the CoM and foot relative to the support foot, the unknown base linear velocity cancels out completely in the algebra. This yields the first deployable dynamic-CoM observation reconstructible from on-board encoders and an IMU gyroscope alone. Paired with a reward library translated term by term from human postural control science prioritizing prevention over repair, the authors built DDC (Deployable Dynamic-CoM).

In a reproducible sim2sim benchmark evaluation where eight leading general policies achieved a 0/90 (0%) success rate, DDC achieved a clean single-leg stance success rate of 89/90 (98.9%). Furthermore, without any teacher-student distillation, DDC was deployed zero-shot directly to a real Unitree G1, stably maintaining single-leg balance across deep squats and high-kick poses.
contributions: Derived and deployed the first dynamic CoM (capture point) observation reconstructible purely from on-board sensors, by canceling base linear velocity through a support-foot-relative formulation.
Designed a reward library grounded in human postural control science (spatial/temporal margins and joint hierarchy) that prioritizes fall prevention over post-failure recovery.
Achieved a unified single-leg balance policy, DDC, that maintains diverse single-leg poses with high accuracy and transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1 without teacher-student distillation.
Released the first method-agnostic, reproducible humanoid single-leg balance benchmark, scoring policies strictly on physical outcomes inside a distinct MuJoCo simulation environment.

sections.heading: Why Do Acrobatic Humanoids Stumble on One Leg?
sections.summary: While recent whole-body tracking policies perform acrobatic motions, they fail across the board on the fundamental single-leg balance test. The root cause is the hardware actor's inability to observe the capture point; this work removes that barrier with a new observation design and benchmark.
sections.details:
Recent reinforcement learning for humanoid whole-body control has reached a level where robots can run and flip by imitating large-scale motion data. However, when subjected to single-leg balance—the foundation of human motor skills and a demanding stress test—their true limitations are exposed. When eight released state-of-the-art general whole-body tracking policies from 2024 to 2026 were evaluated, not a single one held a clean single-leg stance across 90 single-leg test motions (0/90).

To be sure, these policies do not immediately collapse onto the floor. Instead, they avoid falling by urgently stabbing the lifted foot back onto the ground or making tiny hops with the stance foot. In other words, they have the robustness (recovery capability) to salvage a compromised posture, but lack the fundamental capability to prevent imbalance and remain stationary in the first place.

In human postural control science, it has long been known that the key to preventing falls is the capture point (xCoM), which augments the center of mass (CoM) position with its velocity term. In learning-based robot control, however, a deployability barrier exists: on-board sensors cannot directly measure the pelvis (base) absolute linear velocity needed to compute the capture point. Consequently, prior work settled for static CoM positions that ignore velocity or relied on distillation from privileged critics.

This paper's core breakthrough addresses this issue directly. When the capture point is expressed relative to the support foot center, the unknown base linear velocity cancels out completely through subtraction. This provides a dynamic-CoM observation reconstructible on hardware in real time from on-board joint encoders, an IMU gyro, and a known link-mass model alone. Combining this observation with rewards derived from human postural control science, this work proposes DDC, a policy that operates stably on a real Unitree G1.

sections.heading: Deployability Barriers and Insights from Human Postural Science
sections.summary: Prior balance representations were either limited to static CoM or kept dynamic signals as privileged information requiring distillation. This work incorporates biomechanics and human postural control principles while providing an objective, software-reproducible benchmark.
sections.details:
This section organizes related prior work and the paper's positioning across three perspectives:

- Balance Signals and Their Deployability Barrier:
RL-based whole-body tracking methods such as BeyondMimic have enabled advanced skills in systems like HuB, KungfuBot, and AMS. However, improved tracking accuracy does not inherently prevent falling. The capture point, widely used in biomechanics and bipedal control, has been avoided as an input for learned actors due to the difficulty of state estimation on hardware. Frameworks like HuB and AMS restrict balance rewards to static CoM positions (checking whether the CoM lies inside the support polygon) or rely on teacher-to-student distillation from a privileged critic. This work eliminates this fundamental observation barrier, allowing the actor to directly observe dynamic CoM.

- Leveraging Human Postural Control Science:
Human balance control follows an ankle $\to$ knee $\to$ hip corrective hierarchy: small perturbations are arrested at the ankle, while larger disturbances engage the knee and hip. In addition to a spatial Margin of Stability (MoS), human balance relies heavily on Time-to-Boundary (TTB)—the predicted time remaining before crossing the support boundary—and jerk minimization for smooth motion. This work systematically translates these principles, previously applied only piecemeal in robot RL, into a reward library and evaluation metrics.

- Benchmarks for Humanoid Control and Balance:
Existing benchmarks have focused on skill acquisition within a single simulator or classic controller tests on hardware perturbation rigs. While published papers often report cherry-picked demonstrations using closed-source code and proprietary metrics, no software evaluation framework existed to fairly compare released policies under identical physical criteria across different simulators.

sections.heading: Support-Foot Frame Shift and a Prevention-First Reward Library
sections.summary: By expressing position and velocity relative to the support foot, unmeasurable base linear velocity cancels out, enabling real-world observation. The policy is trained with a human-derived reward library enforcing spatial and temporal capture point margins and ankle-first corrections.
sections.details:
The core of the proposed Deployable Dynamic-CoM (DDC) method lies in its observation design and human-inspired reward structure.

### 3.1 Deployable Dynamic-CoM Observation
To first approximation, single-leg balance can be modeled via the Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP) dynamics. Letting the whole-body CoM be $c$, the support foot center be $s$, and the natural pendulum frequency be $\omega_0 = \sqrt{g/h}$, the capture point is $\xi = c + \dot{c}/\omega_0$. If $\xi$ lies inside the base of support, the robot can come to a stop. Defining the relative position as $r = c - s$, during single support when the stance foot is stationary on the ground, the support-relative capture point state is governed by $(r, \dot{r})$. Here, the velocity $\dot{r}$ is crucial. With a foot margin of less than 3 cm on either side, a CoM positioned at the edge is safe if moving inward, but doomed to fall if moving outward. Without velocity, impending balance loss cannot be detected.

Why is this measurable on hardware? In the world frame, each link's position is the sum of base position $p_b$ and relative displacement: $p_b + R d_i(q)$. Differentiating with respect to time introduces the base absolute linear velocity $v_b$. However, taking the difference between CoM $c$ and support foot position $s$ eliminates $v_b$ completely via subtraction. Consequently, the relative position $r^B$ and relative velocity $\dot{r}^B$ in the base frame are fully computable using only joint positions $q$, joint velocities $\dot{q}$, IMU angular velocity $\omega^B$, and a known kinematics/mass model. The actor receives dynamic CoM directly on hardware without requiring a state estimator.

### 3.2 Human Postural Control-Inspired Reward Library
Rather than recovering from loss of balance, the reward library prioritizes prevention—keeping balance intact from the start.

- Spatial and Temporal Margins (MoS and TTB):
The framework introduces a spatial Margin of Stability penalty when the capture point nears the support boundary, along with a Time-to-Boundary penalty when the predicted time to boundary crossing drops below a reaction threshold. Implementing these as soft penalties rather than hard constraints preserves natural motion while establishing safety buffers.

- Joint Correction Hierarchy (Ankle $\to$ Knee $\to$ Hip):
Mirroring human motor control, minor oscillations are resolved primarily at the ankle. Joint angular acceleration penalties on the stance leg are weighted most heavily at the ankle, moderately at the knee, and apply only baseline penalties at the hip. Penalizing rapid changes rather than ankle torque usage encourages smooth, sustained torques and avoids jitter.

- Jerk Penalty:
Penalizing the second difference of actions (jerk) suppresses high-frequency chatter that damages physical actuators.

sections.heading: Building a Simulator-Agnostic, No-Cheat Balance Benchmark
sections.summary: Nine hundred single-leg motion clips from the AMS dataset were categorized into a 3x3 grid across pelvis height and lifted foot height. Evaluated in MuJoCo outside the training simulators, policy performance is graded into Perfect, Marginal, and Failure tiers based purely on physical outcomes.
sections.details:
Prior single-leg balance research lacked standardized comparisons, with closed-source code and cherry-picked successful demos evaluated under idiosyncratic metrics. This work introduces an open, rigorous benchmark to address this gap.

### 4.1 Stratified Single-Leg Motion Dataset
From the AMS synthetic balance dataset (filtered to remove ground-penetration artifacts), 900 clips (4.98 seconds each at 50 Hz) were sampled evenly. To evaluate difficulty uniformly, trajectories were stratified along two orthogonal axes based on average values across the clip: stance-leg flexion (absolute pelvis height) and swing-leg lift (absolute lifted foot height). This forms a $3\times 3 = 9$ grid of classes (100 clips each, with a 50:50 left-right stance ratio), split without leakage into 720 train, 90 validation, and 90 test motions.

### 4.2 Shared Harness and Sim2Sim Evaluation
The benchmark interfaces directly at the robot's low-level command boundary (LowState $\to$ LowCmd). Rather than relying on internal tracking rewards, policies are scored solely on external physical outcomes. Furthermore, testing is conducted inside MuJoCo—a distinct simulator from the ones used during policy training—ensuring a strict, un-overfitted sim2sim evaluation.

### 4.3 Evaluation Tiers
Outcomes are categorized into three mutually exclusive tiers:
- Perfect (clean hold): Across the single-support window, the stance foot never hops (leaves the ground), the swing foot never touches down, no fall occurs, and average position tracking error across 12 key joints remains within 0.5 m of the target pose.
- Marginal (recovery): The robot avoids falling, but regains balance by hopping on the stance foot or momentarily touching down the swing foot. This is treated as stepping recovery rather than true single-leg balance.
- Failure (fall): The base height drops below half its nominal value or pelvis tilt exceeds 1 radian.

sections.heading: A Commanding 89/90 Benchmark Score and Clean Hardware Balance
sections.summary: While eight state-of-the-art general policies scored 0/90 in the Perfect tier, DDC achieved an 89/90 (98.9%) clean balance rate. Ablations confirmed dynamic CoM as the primary performance driver, and the policy transferred zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated eight published state-of-the-art general whole-body tracking policies from 2024–2026 (ProtoMotions, GMT, TWIST, SONIC, OmniXtreme, MOSAIC, Humanoid-GPT, HoloMotion) as baselines.

### 5.1 & 5.5 Key Benchmark Results
Strikingly, under clean, noise-free conditions, all eight general policies achieved a Perfect success rate of 0/90 (0%). These policies do not simply collapse; for instance, SONIC limits falls to 18.9% and reaches the Marginal tier in 81% of trials. However, its survival relies entirely on shuffling between swing-foot touch-downs and stance-foot hops, failing to hold a clean single-leg balance in any test.

In contrast, DDC achieved a Perfect rate of 89/90 (98.9%), with 0% Marginal and only 1.1% Failure. Its single failure occurred in the challenging medium-pelvis $\times$ high-swing-lift class. Examining the Margin of Stability (MoS), baseline policies consistently breached stability boundaries (negative MoS), whereas DDC maintained positive margins anterior-posteriorly and hovered near zero mediolaterally, balancing right at the foot boundary.

### 5.2 Training Rewards Do Not Select the Best Checkpoint
Saturated training reward curves showed little correlation with actual sim2sim balance performance. The best checkpoint identified by running the benchmark across all iterations (at 262k steps) was neither the final step nor the step with the highest training reward, highlighting the need for objective benchmark evaluation.

### 5.4 Ablation Analysis: What Drives Performance?
Ablation studies isolating individual components revealed that the dynamic-CoM observation is the primary performance driver. Removing it dropped the Perfect rate from 98.9% to 55.6% ($-43$ points), while stripping the velocity term to leave only static CoM dropped performance to 66.7% ($-32$ points). Under deployment noise, removing dynamic CoM led to a collapse down to 8.6%. The Time-to-Boundary (TTB) reward contributed a $-26$ point drop when removed, and removing jerk penalties cost $-17$ points, demonstrating the necessity of each design choice.

### 5.6 Real-Robot Hardware Deployment
The benchmark-selected checkpoint was exported to ONNX and deployed directly onto a 29-DoF Unitree G1 at 50 Hz. Driven purely by dynamic CoM reconstructed from on-board sensors without privileged state estimation, the robot maintained clean, steady single-leg balance across diverse, challenging static poses.

captions.F5: Heatmaps of failure rates across the 3x3 pose grid. (a) DDC shows zero failures across all bins except for a single clip in the mid-pelvis, high-swing category, while (b) the baseline average failure rate deteriorates up to 94% toward deep squats and high swing-foot lifts.
captions.F4: Single-leg balance on the real Unitree G1. Deployed directly without distillation, the policy maintains balance across deep crouches and high lateral leg extensions.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Outlook: Making Balance a Foundational Capability
sections.summary: This work establishes a deployable single-leg balance policy and benchmark using support-relative dynamic CoM and prevention rewards. Future work will expand to quantitative hardware trials, additional platforms, and integration into general whole-body policies.
sections.details:
A limitation of this study is that its strict quantitative benchmark evaluation is confined to sim2sim in MuJoCo, whereas physical robot validation remains qualitative. Future efforts will target quantitative disturbance-rejection experiments on hardware and expand the benchmark to humanoid platforms beyond the Unitree G1.

In conclusion, the paper addresses a core capability missing in modern agile humanoid policies—true single-leg balance—via an elegant support-foot-relative dynamic CoM observation. Combined with reward designs rooted in human postural control, DDC delivers distillation-free hardware transfer alongside high benchmark performance. By open-sourcing the codebase, dataset, and benchmark suite, this work provides the foundation to elevate humanoid balance from an isolated task trick into a measurable, general capability across the field.

sections.heading: Appendix: The Mathematics Behind Base Velocity Cancellation
sections.summary: Mathematical derivation showing how the support-foot-relative dynamic CoM observation cancels unmeasurable base velocity, alongside details on actor and critic observation spaces.
sections.details:
This section outlines the mathematical derivation of base velocity cancellation, the theoretical core of the paper.

Let link forward kinematics in the base frame be $d_i(q)$, base world orientation rotation matrix be $R$, and base origin position be $p_b^W$. The world position of link $i$ is $p_i^W = p_b^W + R d_i(q)$. Differentiating with respect to time yields the link's world velocity:
$$\dot{p}_i^W = v_b^W + R (\omega^B \times d_i(q) + J_i(q) \dot{q})$$
where $v_b^W = \dot{p}_b^W$ is base linear velocity, $J_i$ is the link Jacobian, and $\omega^B$ is base angular velocity measured by the on-board gyro.

Defining the whole-body CoM proxy $\tilde{c}$ (the mass-weighted average of link frame origins) and support foot center $s$ analogously and computing their difference causes the common additive base linear velocity term $v_b^W$ to cancel out completely. Transforming this vector back into the base frame yields relative position $r^B$ and relative velocity $\dot{r}^B$, computable purely from joint encoders $(q, \dot{q})$, IMU angular velocity $\omega^B$, and the gravity vector.

The actor receives this 4D deployable dynamic-CoM signal alongside proprioception, command targets, and future reference trajectories. Meanwhile, the critic has access to privileged world-frame base states during training within an asymmetric actor-critic (FastSAC) setup, balancing training stability with hardware deployability.

takeaways: Unmeasurable state variables like base linear velocity can be eliminated and observed by shifting coordinates relative to the contact reference frame (the stance foot).
Fall prevention during single-leg stance requires velocity-extrapolated center of mass (capture point); feeding dynamic CoM directly to the actor is critical.
Stepping recovery (scrambling to regain balance) and fall prevention (maintaining balance without breaking stance) are fundamentally distinct and must be evaluated separately.
Training reward curves fail to reflect sim2sim balance capability, making physical-outcome-based, cross-simulator benchmarks essential for checkpoint selection.
limitations: Rigorous quantitative benchmark evaluations are limited to sim2sim environments, while real Unitree G1 tests remain qualitative demonstrations.
The dynamic CoM proxy uses link origins rather than exact per-link center-of-mass offsets, introducing a small centimeter-scale discrepancy from the true whole-body CoM.
Evaluation and hardware experiments were conducted solely on the 29-DoF Unitree G1, leaving generalization across differing humanoid kinematics unverified.
